rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending for God is a profitable deal: God keeps it safe, multiplies it, returns it as an everlasting treasure, and adds an honorable reward.
rows.anchor: spending in the way of God incurs no loss; it is an extremely lucrative deal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣadaqah is an active participle for ongoing ordinary charity, while qarḍ is a verb for aid requested in emergencies; the forms reflect their different occasions.
rows.anchor: The first is in the form of an adjective ( ism ul fā‘il) and the second in the form of a verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wives and children can foster miserliness and cowardice, traits that lead a person toward hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: the wife and the kids are very significant factors which contribute to miserliness and cowardice

rows.speaker: Aḥādīth
rows.claim: Hadith reports also describe wives and children as sources of miserliness and cowardice.
rows.anchor: Aḥādīth also mention that the wife and kids become a source of miserliness and cowardice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning women beside men makes clear that God holds each person accountable for their responsibilities, regardless of sex.
rows.anchor: women are also clearly told that God will hold accountable each and every person whether man or woman

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True and strong faith must be shown in deeds; ṣiddīqīn and shuhadā’ are not granted to everyone who merely claims belief, but to those who prove it, especially through generous spending.
rows.anchor: the positions of ṣiddīqīn and the shuhadā’ will not be given by God to every person who claims to be a believer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiddīq describes complete harmony between a person's words and deeds.
rows.anchor: Its real essence is complete harmony between one’s words and deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author illustrates ṣiddīq with a spear whose rings prove secure in practice, like the trustworthy person's word.
rows.anchor: whose rings prove as secure in practice as they seem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ṣiddīq proves his declared aim by sacrificing what he has earned and is expected to testify to truth even at the cost of his life.
rows.anchor: he is ready to sacrifice what he earned from his hands for the veracious objective he had declared to adopt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr is the clearest historical example of proving faith through spending for God in the most precarious circumstances.
rows.anchor: The most prominent person in whom this attribute manifested itself in Islamic history is Abū Bakr (rta)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuhadā’ means witnesses to God's religion before people; this is the ummah’s charge, as stated in the cited verse, with the Messenger witnessing to them.
rows.anchor: so that you be witnesses to the religion of God before the people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who die for God's cause are called shahīd because they fulfill the duty of bearing witness to God's religion with their lives; martyrdom is its greatest testimony.
rows.anchor: the religion of God, hence such a person is called shahīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links this faithful obedience to the promise that the obedient join the Prophets, ṣiddīqīn, shuhadā’, and righteous whom God has blessed.
rows.anchor: those who sincerely obey God and the Prophet shall be among those whom God has blessed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier promise of light and reward applies to people ready to give their lives for this cause.
rows.anchor: the light and reward which is mentioned earlier in verses 11 and 12 is for such people who are ready to lay down their lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, Hell also awaits people who never verbally denied truth but whose deeds contradicted their claims of faith.
rows.anchor: their deeds were in complete contradiction to the claims they made

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns wealth-enslaved hypocrites that worldly amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry for wealth, children, and status will not lead to a favorable end.
rows.anchor: the life of this world ie a sport and a diversion, the fervency will to embellish one self, the quest for greater riches and more children

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like rain that delights the ungrateful before its crop yellows and crumbles, worldly pleasures and competitive efforts all perish.
rows.anchor: it becomes yellow after being withered away and then is crushed to bits and pieces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foolish make worldly pleasure their goal, but the true goal is the Hereafter, where a person faces severe torment or God's forgiveness and acceptance; failure to win God's pleasure entails torment.
rows.anchor: the real goal is the Hereafter, and there they will have to face either of the two things

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: The exegetes parse “the life of this world” as the subject and the remaining clause as its predicate.
rows.anchor: form the inchoative (mubtada’) and the rest of the verse forms the enunciative (khabar)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead treats “sport, diversion, adornment” as an explanatory apposition and the rain simile as the predicate, citing a Qur'anic parallel.
rows.anchor: are a permutative (badal bayān) and the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the exegetes’ reading, the author's analysis does not condemn worldly life collectively; it condemns the worldly attachment that leads disbelievers and hypocrites to Hell, avoiding support for monasticism.
rows.anchor: If my analysis is accepted, then it is not this world collectively which has been regarded as condemnable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly life itself is not condemnable: within God's limits it can secure the eternal Hereafter, while violating them and pursuing pleasure makes it eternal condemnation.
rows.anchor: this worldly life itself is not something condemnable; it is a person’s attitude which makes it condemnable or merciful

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally interpret kuffār here as farmers (zurrā‘).
rows.anchor: Exegetes generally regard it to refer to farmers ( zurrā‘)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the rare farmer sense: root possibility alone cannot override customary Qur'anic usage when no other Qur'anic example supports it.
rows.anchor: this word is not customarily used for this purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes kuffār in its established sense of disbelievers, as 48:29 uses the term in its specific meanings; the transient world's lure targets those who disbelieve in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: For this reason, it seems to me that the word kuffār is used in its actual meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A word in a simile can identify the people the comparison targets; recognizing this makes the parable's intended beauty evident.
rows.anchor: at times certain words are inserted in similes and parables which are meant to point to people who are in consideration in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should redirect rivalry from temporary riches toward earning God's forgiveness and Paradise, whose vastness equals the heavens and earth and which is prepared for sincere believers.
rows.anchor: the objective of the believers should be the forgiveness of God and to please Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for Paradise's vastness denotes length and breadth, while samā’ means the whole category of skies and appears in plural in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: is used here that it refers to “the length and breadth” that is vastness and enormity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is already prepared for believers and will be unveiled when life's trial ends; God's grace can reward a few days of virtue with immense bliss.
rows.anchor: As soon as the trial of this world ends, the Paradise of each person will be unveiled before him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every good or bad event is already written before it occurs; God's knowledge encompasses present and future, so recording a creation's fate before creating it is easy for Him.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has written every good or bad thing that will befall in a book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since wealth is God's gift, protecting it from God through stinginess is foolish; the proper response is to meet one's spending duty and trust God for future relief.
rows.anchor: How can someone save something from someone who has in fact bestowed it upon him?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites and misers fear future financial need and use it to justify withholding; the remedy for coming hardship is giving for God's cause and trusting Him.
rows.anchor: they justified their miserliness to be a remedy for future hardships and calamities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two kinds of trial are harm to land's produce and harm to a person's body; both are destined, so one cannot evade spending wealth or life for God.
rows.anchor: The trials which a person faces in this world are generally of these two categories

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death cannot be evaded: even those who hide in strong castles will be found by it.
rows.anchor: even if they hide in strong castles death will find them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book in which fate is written is also called the guarded tablet and means God's knowledge.
rows.anchor: It is also called the guarded tablet and in fact means the knowledge of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human knowledge is too limited to grasp universal foreknowledge, but God created the universe, knows everything, and knows each person's course and destination.
rows.anchor: His knowledge embraces everything. He knows every phase a person will pass through and the destination he will ultimately reach

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted clause means believers should not grieve over loss or boast over gain: endure calamity patiently as ordained with wisdom and thank God for blessings rather than crediting personal skill.
rows.anchor: you do not express sorrow on something which you lose and neither should you express pride on something you receive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative phrase “God does not love” implicitly conveys severe anger; stated positively, its force would be that God hates the arrogant and proud.
rows.anchor: The words “not like” though are apparently soft yet they are very severe as per their meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who credit wealth to their own planning spend on show and rivalry but regard giving for God's cause as a loss.
rows.anchor: they think that except for spending on their own show and pomp and on outdoing others in acquiring wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here amr means giving advice: misers warn those who spend for religious and public causes that future financial constraints will make them regret it.
rows.anchor: here means “to give advice,” a common usage of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning to those who turn away is threatening indifference: God needs nothing, and calls people to spend so they can earn eternal reward, as verse 18 indicated.
rows.anchor: if even after this reminder and exhortation, these people continue to desist, then they should remember that God is indifferent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pairing ghanī with ḥamīd shows God asks from no need but invites people to become worthy of blessing, transforming their small gifts into far greater returns.
rows.anchor: He wants people to become worthy of His blessings and convert the pebbles they give to Him into pearls and return these to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section answers a People of the Book objection, especially Christian: believers were urged to spend for jihad, but opponents argued that a religious community should pursue peace rather than war.
rows.anchor: The spending for the cause of God to which the believers were urged related to jihād, as is evident from the context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Muslims' victories in Medina, Quraysh and People of the Book used a dominant monastic ideal to spread propaganda against Muslim jihad; at Badr Quraysh mocked the Prophet's claim to be God's Messenger.
rows.anchor: at the time of the battle of Badr, they taunted the Prophet (sws) that how can he be God’s Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites' objections concerned the destruction of Banū Naḍīr's orchards and fay distribution; the Anṣār and Muhājirūn are praised for contentment, unlike the hypocrites.
rows.anchor: The attitude of contentment shown on this distribution by the Anṣā r and the Muhā jirūn, in sharp contrast with that of the hypocrites, is praised

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Banū Naḍīr's exile, hypocrites urged Banū Qurayẓah to break its covenant, promising support and exile alongside them, but the promise was false; the author compares them with Satan abandoning a sinner.
rows.anchor: They are only doing what Satan does: after a person commits a sin on his incitement, he withdraws by proclaiming his acquittal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banū Qurayẓah is warned that breaking its covenant under hypocrite encouragement will bring the same fate as Banū Naḍīr.
rows.anchor: their fate will be no different from that of the Banū Naḍīr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage warns believers, especially hypocrites, to remember Judgment Day: forgetting God means forgetting life's purpose and fate, and only Paradise's inhabitants attain true success.
rows.anchor: the believers in general and the hypocrites in particular, are warned to always keep in mind the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth has been fully revealed, so continued denial is stubbornness; the Qur'an would shatter a mountain with awe, and unresponsive hearts reveal their own hardness rather than any fault in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: If their hearts are not being influenced by its message, then it is not the fault of the Qur’ān; rather, it is due to their own hardheartedness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's final divine attributes encourage submission and trust in strong believers, resolve and confidence in weak believers, and fear of God in hypocrites; the ending returns to the opening note.
rows.anchor: The sūrah finally ends on the note it began

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening glorification verse recurs with slight variation at the sūrah's end; the intervening facts substantiate its claim and God's attributes, as well as the claim of the preceding Sūrah al-Ḥadīd.
rows.anchor: with slight variation, it occurs both at the beginning and at the end of this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creation glorifies God and testifies that the Creator has no weakness or partner, controls all things, and acts with wisdom; people should trust, obey, fear, and hope in Him alone.
rows.anchor: every object of this universe glorifies the Almighty and, by submitting to and serving Him, bears witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grasping these facts produces true faith and resolve; failing to appreciate them opens hearts to hypocrisy, disbelief, and polytheism and disorders beliefs and practices.
rows.anchor: if the facts are not properly appreciated, then hypocrisy, disbelief and polytheism are provided a path to enter the hearts

rows.speaker: exegetes
rows.claim: The exegetes identify the expelled disbelievers as the Jews of Banū Naḍīr near Madinah.
rows.anchor: refer to the Jews of the Banū Naḍīr, who lived nearby Mad īnah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following al-Bukhārī, the author recounts that Banū Naḍīr violated its treaty and plotted against the Prophet; after first agreeing to leave, it resisted when ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy promised backing from his men and other allies.
rows.anchor: as per the details recorded by al-Bukhārī, although they had made a peace-treaty with the Prophet (sws), five months after the battle of Badr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet besieged Banū Naḍīr after its allies failed to help; the group was forced to leave, taking what it could on camels for Khaybar and Adhẓra‘āt, while its remaining property was taken.
rows.anchor: neither did the Banū Qurayẓah come to their rescue nor did the Quraysh and the Banū Ghaṭfān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first ḥashr is Banū Naḍīr's exile; the wording warns of another exile under ʿUmar and the greatest gathering still to come.
rows.anchor: this exile of theirs was the first ḥashr they will be facing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address reminds the hypocrites that they trusted Banū Naḍīr's strength and its allies' support, assuming no one could dislodge them.
rows.anchor: They are told that they had great trust in the power and strength of the Banū Na ḍīr
